domains.summary: Operating AWS workloads: CloudWatch monitoring and alarming, Systems Manager automation, deployment strategies, and systematic troubleshooting of EC2 and application issues. Vendor-neutral study aid. Not affiliated with AWS; this course confers no certification.

scenarios.title: The 3 AM Page
scenarios.situation: An on-call engineer gets paged for high CPU on a web instance — but the alarm fired on a single 1-minute spike during a deploy, and the instance was healthy. The team wants fewer false pages.
scenarios.prompt: How should the CloudWatch alarm be configured to page only on real problems?
evidence: CloudWatch alarms

Alarms evaluate a metric against a threshold over N datapoints within an evaluation period. SNS topics deliver notifications. EC2 default metrics arrive every 5 minutes unless detailed monitoring (1 minute) is enabled.
choices: Require the threshold breached for multiple consecutive datapoints (e.g., 3 of 3 five-minute periods), treat missing data sensibly, and page via SNS only on the ALARM state.
Set the threshold lower and the period to 10 seconds so the alarm fires even faster.
Page on every single datapoint above threshold; faster pages are always better.
Disable the alarm and rely on engineers noticing CloudWatch dashboards.
scenarios.why: Alarm quality is a tuning problem: demanding sustained breach across several datapoints filters out deploy spikes and momentary noise, while paging on ALARM state via SNS keeps the signal clean. Hair-trigger single-datapoint alarms train teams to ignore pages — the opposite of reliability.
scenarios.hint: Was the instance actually unhealthy, or was the measurement just noisy?

scenarios.title: Patch Tuesday at Scale
scenarios.situation: A company runs 200 EC2 instances across three accounts. Today an engineer SSHes into each one to run updates by hand — it takes days, some get missed, and there is no record of what changed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right way to patch the fleet?
evidence: Systems Manager

Patch Manager automates OS patching with baselines and maintenance windows. Run Command executes commands across many instances without SSH. State Manager enforces configuration. All require the SSM Agent and an IAM instance profile.
choices: Systems Manager Patch Manager with patch baselines and maintenance windows, using Run Command for ad-hoc fixes — no SSH, with full compliance reporting.
Keep SSHing but write a bash for-loop over the instance list to go faster.
Open RDP/SSH to the internet on all instances so patching tools can reach them directly.
Rebuild every AMI from scratch monthly and replace all instances at once.
scenarios.why: Patch Manager turns a multi-day manual slog into a scheduled, auditable, exception-reported process — baselines define approved patches, maintenance windows control timing, and compliance dashboards prove coverage to auditors. Manual SSH scales with headcount, not with fleets, and internet-open admin ports trade one problem for a worse one.
scenarios.hint: What would the auditor ask for: a spreadsheet of memories, or a compliance report?

scenarios.title: SSH Is Closed. Now What?
scenarios.situation: Security just closed port 22 on all security groups fleet-wide. An engineer needs shell access to a misbehaving instance in a private subnet with no bastion host.
scenarios.prompt: How does the engineer get in without reopening SSH?
evidence: Session Manager

SSM Session Manager gives browser/CLI shell access through the SSM Agent over HTTPS — no inbound ports, no bastion, no keys. Sessions are logged to S3/CloudWatch Logs, and access is controlled by IAM.
choices: Use SSM Session Manager: the instance needs the SSM Agent and an IAM role with AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore; connect via the console or AWS CLI with sessions logged.
Temporarily re-add 0.0.0.0/0 on port 22, fix the issue, then remove it — quick and reversible.
Stop the instance, detach the root volume, attach it to another instance, and edit files directly.
Rebuild the instance from the AMI; shell access is unnecessary if the AMI is correct.
scenarios.why: Session Manager was built for exactly this: secure shell access with zero open inbound ports, IAM-controlled, and fully audited — closing port 22 fleet-wide only works if there is a replacement, and this is it. Temporary 0.0.0.0/0 SSH is how breaches start, and volume surgery is slow overkill for a shell session.
scenarios.hint: What port does the SSM Agent use — and is it inbound or outbound?

scenarios.title: Status Check Failed
scenarios.situation: An EC2 instance stops responding. The console shows 'Instance status check: failed' but 'System status check: passed'. A teammate suggests stopping and starting the instance 'to move it to new hardware.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct diagnosis and action?
evidence: Status checks

System status check failure = AWS infrastructure problem (host hardware/network) — stop/start migrates to healthy hardware. Instance status check failure = guest OS problem (kernel panic, bad config, exhausted resources) — reboot or fix the OS.
choices: Instance check failed means the guest OS is at fault: reboot the instance or troubleshoot the OS (check system log, memory/disk); stop/start for new hardware only helps system-check failures.
Stop and start immediately — new hardware fixes every kind of status check failure.
Terminate the instance; any failed status check means the hardware is dead.
Wait — status checks always clear themselves within an hour without action.
scenarios.why: The two checks exist to split responsibility: passed system check exonerates AWS hardware, so the fault is inside the guest — rebooting or fixing the OS is the remedy, while stop/start migration would just move a sick OS to a new host. Reading the check pair correctly saves the team from 'fixing' the wrong layer.
scenarios.hint: Which check would fail if the hypervisor host lost power?

scenarios.title: Deploy Without Downtime
scenarios.situation: A team deploys a stateful web app with database schema changes. Past in-place deploys caused mixed-version servers writing incompatible rows, and rollbacks were manual and scary.
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment approach minimizes downtime and rollback risk?
evidence: Strategies

Rolling: replace instances gradually. Blue/green: run two full environments, shift traffic, keep old as instant rollback. Canary: shift a small % first. In-place: update on existing hosts. Schema changes must be backward-compatible (expand then contract).
choices: Blue/green with backward-compatible (expand/contract) database migrations: shift traffic via the load balancer, validate, and keep the blue environment as an instant rollback target.
In-place deployment on all servers simultaneously — fastest, and the schema change applies everywhere at once.
Rolling deployment with the new code and breaking schema change applied together per server.
Deploy Friday night when traffic is low, so any incompatibility affects fewer users.
scenarios.why: Blue/green gives you a tested, fully separate environment and a one-step rollback (shift traffic back), while expand/contract migrations keep old and new code writing compatible rows during the transition. In-place and rolling with breaking schema changes create the exact mixed-version corruption the team already suffered — and Friday-night deploys just move the blast radius in time, not in risk.
scenarios.hint: If the deploy fails at 50%, how do you get back — and what did the database see meanwhile?

scenarios.title: The Runaway Log Disk
scenarios.situation: A fleet of app servers periodically fills its log disk, crashing the app. Engineers want automatic detection and remediation without waking anyone for the routine case.
scenarios.prompt: What is the best automated response?
evidence: Building blocks

CloudWatch agent collects disk/memory metrics EC2 doesn't emit by default. CloudWatch alarms trigger on thresholds. EventBridge routes events; SSM Automation runbooks execute remediation steps like clearing logs or restarting services.
choices: CloudWatch agent publishes disk metrics, an alarm fires on high disk usage, and an SSM Automation runbook archives/rotates logs and restarts the service — paging a human only if remediation fails.
A cron job on each server deletes all logs nightly at midnight.
Set a CloudWatch alarm on CPU and have it reboot the instance when logs fill up.
Give every engineer SNS alerts on disk metrics and let whoever is awake handle it.
scenarios.why: The mature pattern is detect-decide-remediate: custom disk metrics (EC2 doesn't emit them natively) feed an alarm, and an audited runbook does the routine fix the same way every time, escalating only on failure. Blind cron deletion destroys forensic evidence, CPU alarms don't measure disk, and human-triage-at-scale is how routine issues become 3 AM pages.
scenarios.hint: Which metric actually measures the problem — and who should do the boring fix?

domains.name: Cloud Operations on AWS
domains.summary: Running AWS well day to day: monitoring and observability, cost optimization and FinOps, incident response, and the Well-Architected Framework as an operational compass. Vendor-neutral study aid. Not affiliated with AWS; this course confers no certification.

scenarios.title: Tag or Lose It
scenarios.situation: Finance asks which team owns a $40k/month 'unattributed' line in Cost Explorer. Resources were launched fast with no tags, and three teams all claim innocence.
scenarios.prompt: What fixes cost attribution going forward?
evidence: Cost allocation

Cost allocation tags (aws:createdBy, custom keys like Team, Project, Environment) flow into Cost Explorer and CUR. Tag policies and SCPs can enforce required tags at creation time. Untagged past spend often stays unattributed.
choices: Define a mandatory tag schema (Team, Project, Environment), enforce it with tag policies/SCPs so untagged resources can't launch, and backfill what can be identified.
Ask each team to self-report their spend monthly on the honor system.
Create one AWS account per team retroactively and migrate resources.
Accept unattributed spend as the price of agility; tagging slows launches.
scenarios.why: Attribution is a creation-time problem: enforcement at launch (tag policies, SCPs) guarantees every future dollar is labeled, while a defined schema keeps tags consistent enough to report on. Self-reporting doesn't reconcile, and per-team accounts are a migration project, not a tagging fix.
scenarios.hint: When is the cheapest moment to label a resource — at launch, or during an audit?

scenarios.title: The Idle Fleet
scenarios.situation: Compute Optimizer flags 60% of the EC2 fleet as over-provisioned, and dev/test instances run 24/7 though engineers work 8x5. The bill keeps climbing while utilization falls.
scenarios.prompt: What is the highest-impact remediation sequence?
evidence: Rightsizing levers
Compute Optimizer recommends instance types from utilization history. Instance Scheduler / Lambda can stop-start dev instances on a schedule. Savings Plans discount the remaining steady baseline.
choices: Rightsize per Compute Optimizer, put dev/test on automated stop-start schedules, then cover the smaller steady-state baseline with Savings Plans.
Buy Savings Plans first for the current fleet, then think about rightsizing later.
Move everything to bigger instances so utilization percentages look better.
Delete the dev environments entirely; developers can share one instance.
scenarios.why: Order matters: committing to today's oversized fleet locks in waste at a discount, while rightsizing and scheduling first shrink the baseline that commitments then cover. Bigger instances worsen the waste, and deleting dev environments trades cost for velocity.
scenarios.hint: Should you sign a 3-year commitment on capacity you haven't finished shrinking?

scenarios.title: Budgets With Teeth
scenarios.situation: A team blew past its quarterly cloud budget in month two. Leadership wants hard enforcement: 'shut things down when the budget hits.' Finance wants alerts, not outages.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right control design?
evidence: Budget controls

AWS Budgets sends alerts (email, SNS, Chatbot) at thresholds — it notifies, it does not enforce. Enforcement comes from SCPs, IAM policies, and automation (e.g., budget-triggered Lambda via EventBridge/Budgets Actions). Hard auto-shutdown risks production outages.
choices: AWS Budgets with tiered alerts (50/80/100% via SNS) plus Budgets Actions or SCP guardrails on non-production accounts; keep production protected from automated shutdown.
One budget alert at 100% that terminates all EC2 instances in the account automatically.
No budgets — engineers should just watch the billing console daily.
Give every developer the root credentials so anyone can check spend anytime.
scenarios.why: Budgets are tripwires, not brakes: tiered alerts give humans time to act, while automated enforcement belongs on non-production where a shutdown is an inconvenience, not an outage. Auto-terminating production on a budget threshold converts a cost problem into a revenue problem.
scenarios.hint: What happens to customers if the enforcement fires during peak traffic?

scenarios.title: Well-Architected Review
scenarios.situation: A workload has never had an architecture review. The team runs the Well-Architected Tool and gets 40 findings across all six pillars, from missing backups to no cost tags. They're overwhelmed.
evidence: Well-Architected

Six pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability. The Tool flags high/medium risks per question; best practice is fixing high-risk items first, especially security and reliability.
choices: Fix high-risk findings first — security and reliability risks (backups, access control, AZ redundancy) before cost and sustainability optimizations.
Fix the easiest findings first to get the count down quickly for the report.
Fix all Cost Optimization findings first since they fund the rest.
Skip the review; 40 findings means the tool is too strict for a real workload.
scenarios.why: Risk order beats convenience order: a missing backup or open access path can end the business, while untagged resources merely annoy finance. High-risk security and reliability items are existential; cost findings are important but not urgent in the same way.
scenarios.hint: Which findings could end the company this quarter?

scenarios.title: Incident at 2 AM
scenarios.situation: A payment service starts failing. The responder SSHes into servers, restarts things by feel, fixes it in 90 minutes — and nobody learns anything because nothing was recorded. It recurs monthly.
scenarios.prompt: What operational practice breaks this cycle?
evidence: Incident practice

Runbooks: pre-written diagnostic/remediation steps. EventBridge + SSM Automation: automatic detection and remediation. Blameless postmortems: record timeline, root cause, and action items. On-call rotations with clear escalation.
choices: Codified runbooks plus automated detection/remediation (EventBridge to SSM Automation), followed by a blameless postmortem with tracked action items after every incident.
Give the best responder a raise; heroics are the reliability strategy.
Restart all servers nightly as preventive maintenance.
Page the whole team for every alert so more eyes see each incident.
scenarios.why: Reliability is a system property, not a hero property: runbooks make the fix repeatable, automation handles the known-knowns without waking anyone, and blameless postmortems convert each incident into permanent prevention. Heroics don't scale and don't teach; nightly restarts mask root causes.
scenarios.hint: What would the next responder do differently at 2 AM with a runbook in hand?

scenarios.title: Commitment Math
scenarios.situation: A workload mixes: 40% steady baseline (web tier 24/7), 35% business-hours batch, 25% unpredictable spikes. Finance wants maximum commitment discount; engineering fears lock-in on the wrong capacity.
scenarios.prompt: What is the defensible commitment strategy?
evidence: Commitments

Savings Plans/Reserved Instances discount committed usage up to ~72%. Cover the steady baseline you are certain about; keep variable load on On-Demand/Spot. Coverage and utilization reports in Cost Explorer show waste. Convertible RIs / flexible Savings Plans hedge against change.
choices: Commit (Savings Plans) only to the steady 40% baseline; run business-hours batch on scheduled On-Demand or Spot, spikes on On-Demand — then track coverage/utilization monthly.
Commit to 100% of current usage for the maximum discount; growth only increases usage.
Avoid all commitments; flexibility is worth paying full On-Demand price forever.
Put the unpredictable spikes on Spot with no fallback to maximize savings.
scenarios.why: Commitments reward certainty and punish guesses: the steady baseline is safe to commit, while batch and spikes are definitionally variable — committing to them buys discounts on capacity you won't use. Monthly coverage reviews keep the commitment matched to reality as the workload evolves.
scenarios.hint: Which 40% would you bet a year of budget on — and which 25% wouldn't you?

lessons.title: AWS SysOps Administrator — Core concepts
concepts: CloudWatch is the operational nervous system: metrics and alarms for thresholds, Logs for centralized log analysis, Events/EventBridge for reacting to state changes, and dashboards for shared situational awareness. EC2 emits basic metrics every 5 minutes; the CloudWatch agent adds memory, disk, and application metrics.

Systems Manager replaces SSH-and-hope fleet management: Patch Manager for OS updates, Run Command for fleet-wide commands, Session Manager for portless shell access, State Manager for configuration enforcement, and Parameter Store/Secrets Manager for configuration and secrets.

Choose deployment strategies by blast radius: in-place is cheapest but riskiest, rolling limits concurrent exposure, blue/green gives instant rollback at double capacity cost, and canary validates with real traffic on a small slice. Database migrations must be backward-compatible regardless of strategy.

Troubleshoot in layers: read the status check pair (system vs instance) before touching anything, check the system log and CloudWatch metrics for evidence, change one thing at a time, and prefer automated runbooks over heroic manual fixes for recurring issues.

Tag everything and centralize: consistent tags power cost allocation, automation targeting, and access control; CloudTrail logs every API call for audit; Config records configuration history so you can answer 'what changed?' during incidents.

example.code:
aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm --alarm-name web-cpu-high \
  --metric-name CPUUtilization --namespace AWS/EC2 --statistic Average \
  --period 300 --evaluation-periods 3 --threshold 80 \
  --comparison-operator GreaterThanThreshold \
  --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-0abc123 --alarm-actions arn:aws:sns:us-east-1:123456789012:ops
example.walkthrough: This pages only when CPU averages over 80% for three consecutive 5-minute periods — sustained breach, not spikes. The SNS action routes to the on-call topic. Tune evaluation-periods first whenever an alarm pages too often.

pitfalls: Common trap: alarming on a single datapoint — require consecutive breaches or inherit pager fatigue.
Common trap: assuming EC2 emits disk/memory metrics natively — install the CloudWatch agent for those.
Common trap: using Session Manager without the IAM instance profile — the agent alone is not enough; the role grants the permissions.
Common trap: stop/start as a universal fix — it only helps system-check (hardware) failures, not sick guest OSes.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

lessons.title: Cloud Operations on AWS — Core concepts
concepts: Observability is metrics, logs, and traces together: CloudWatch for the first two, X-Ray for the third, with alarms and dashboards turning telemetry into shared awareness. Alert on symptoms (latency, errors) more than causes (CPU).

FinOps is a loop, not a project: tag everything at creation (enforced by policy), review Cost Explorer and CUR regularly, rightsize with Compute Optimizer, schedule non-production off-hours, then commit to the steady remainder with Savings Plans. In that order.

Budgets notify; policies enforce. AWS Budgets with tiered SNS alerts gives humans time to act, while SCPs, tag policies, and Budgets Actions provide actual guardrails — and automated shutdown belongs on non-production, never as a surprise to customers.

Incidents are handled by systems, not heroes: detection via alarms, codified runbooks and SSM Automation for response, blameless postmortems with tracked action items for learning. Every recurring incident is an automation candidate.

Use the Well-Architected Framework as the review cadence: run the Tool per workload, fix high-risk security and reliability findings first, and re-review after significant changes. The six pillars keep optimization balanced instead of lopsided.

example.code:
aws ce get-cost-and-usage --time-period Start=2026-09-01,End=2026-10-01 \
  --granularity MONTHLY --metrics BlendedCost \
  --group-by Type=DIMENSION,Key=SERVICE | head -40
example.walkthrough: This pulls last month's cost grouped by service — the starting point of every FinOps review. The top services tell you where rightsizing, scheduling, and commitments will actually move the number.

pitfalls: Common trap: committing to Savings Plans before rightsizing — you lock in a discount on waste.
Common trap: treating AWS Budgets as enforcement — it only alerts; something else must act.
Common trap: alerting on CPU instead of user-facing symptoms — the pager fires while customers are fine, and stays silent while they suffer.
Common trap: skipping postmortems when the fix was fast — the incident will recur until its action items are tracked to done.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

labs.title: Page Only on Real Trouble
labs.objective: Create a CloudWatch alarm with multi-datapoint evaluation and an SNS notification action.
steps: Create an SNS topic for ops alerts with `aws sns create-topic`.
Create the alarm with `aws cloudwatch put-metric-alarm`, evaluation-periods 3, period 300.
Describe alarms with `aws cloudwatch describe-alarms` and confirm state and configuration.
Force a state check: verify the alarm action points at your SNS topic ARN.

checks.hint: put-metric-alarm returns an AlarmArn on success — capture it.

labs.title: Command the Fleet Without SSH
labs.objective: Use SSM Run Command to execute a command across instances by tag, with output captured centrally.
steps: Confirm targets: `aws ssm describe-instance-information` filtered to managed instances.
Send a command with `aws ssm send-command --document-name AWS-RunShellScript --targets Key=tag:Env,Values=prod --parameters 'commands=["uptime"]'`.
Poll the invocation with `aws ssm list-command-invocations` until status is Success.
Review per-instance output to confirm the fleet responded uniformly.

checks.hint: send-command returns a CommandId — use it to track the invocation.

labs.title: Find Your Top Spend
labs.objective: Query Cost Explorer from the CLI to identify the services driving the bill.
steps: Run `aws ce get-cost-and-usage` for the last full month grouped by SERVICE.
Identify the top 3 services by BlendedCost.
Re-run grouped by USAGE_TYPE for the top service to see what exactly is billed.
Write one rightsizing or scheduling hypothesis per top service.

checks.hint: Request the BlendedCost metric so results include actual billed amounts.

labs.title: Read Compute Optimizer Findings
labs.objective: Pull rightsizing recommendations and translate them into an action list.
steps: Run `aws compute-optimizer get-ec2-instance-recommendations` for the account.
Note each finding: Overprovisioned, Underprovisioned, or Optimized.
For over-provisioned instances, record the recommended instance type and estimated savings.
Draft the change plan: which to resize, which need load testing first, which to leave.

checks.hint: Each recommendation includes a 'finding' field — filter for Overprovisioned first.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Company facts (verified)
items: Founded 2017 in Orlando, FL — Danny Jenkins (CEO), Sami Jenkins (COO), John Carolan (QA)
Philosophy: deny-by-default / default-deny — approve known-good, deny the rest
Customers: 70,000+ organizations, sold heavily through the MSP channel
Funding: $190M Series F, July 2026 (Elephant-led); ~730 employees
Interview address: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando, FL 32810
Culture: in-office 5 days/week; free lunch; post-offer background + drug screening

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.

checklist: Sixty-second company brief rehearsed out loud: year, city, philosophy, three products, one milestone
Two STAR stories ready: hardest technical problem; a frustrated customer or user
“Why ThreatLocker / why cybersecurity” answer tied to prevention and service, not slogans
Ringfencing explained in one plain-English sentence (the Word-on-a-leash version)
Elevation Control answer ready: just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed, ringfenced, logged
Triage loop memorized: scope → observe → hypothesize → smallest safe change → validate → explain
Three questions to ask them: team on-call shape, approval SLA expectations, what “most helpful” looks like on the team
Logistics: 1901 Summit Tower Blvd, Orlando FL; in-office role; ID and references ready
Define your crown jewels before you model anything.
Build the asset-and-access graph from live sources (scans, configs, identity), not from the CMDB alone.
Model vulnerabilities AND misconfigurations as exploit edges.
Compute shortest attack paths to each crown jewel; name the choke points.
Prioritize remediation by path risk, not by raw severity score.
Express at least one access policy as a relationship path (ReBAC pilot).
Baseline approved communication edges per segment; alert on first-seen edges.
Brief the next incident or risk review with the graph, not a spreadsheet.
Can you explain supervised vs unsupervised vs anomaly detection with a security example for each?
Can you name three log features you would engineer for a C2 detector and why?
Can you walk through a UEBA alert (baseline, deviation, verification) end to end?
Can you explain the precision/recall tradeoff and how you would set a threshold for a fatigued SOC?
Can you define concept drift and describe a retraining process?
Can you distinguish direct vs indirect prompt injection and jailbreaking?
Can you explain tool poisoning in the MCP ecosystem and three controls against it?
Can you describe insecure output handling and how you would validate agent output?
Can you name the three adversarial ML attack classes and one defense for evasion?
Can you design a SOAR playbook gate: what automates freely, what needs human approval?

media.title: Allowlisting vs blocklisting: default-deny vs default-allow
media.caption: Default-deny stops unknown code without a signature; default-allow runs it until one exists.
media.alt: Side-by-side comparison: on the left, a default-deny gate runs known-good payroll software and denies unknown ransomware with no signature needed; on the right, a default-allow gate runs both until the ransomware is recognized as bad.

media.title: Ringfencing: four leashes on an allowed application
media.caption: Word stays approved, but it cannot spawn PowerShell, read the credential store, or reach the internet — while opening its document is allowed.
media.alt: An approved Word application inside a dashed containment ring: arrows show PowerShell launch denied, credential-store registry access denied, external network denied, and document file access allowed.

media.title: The Zero Trust endpoint stack
media.caption: Five deny-by-default layers — Allowlisting, Ringfencing, Elevation, Storage, Network — watched by Web Control, the Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and the Cyber Hero MDR team.
media.alt: A vertical stack of five layers from Allowlisting at the foundation up through Ringfencing, Elevation Control, Storage Control, and Network Control, with side boxes for Web Control, Testing Environment, Unified Audit, and Cyber Hero MDR.

media.title: Application-request triage flow
media.caption: Gather evidence first, then branch: trusted gets a scoped rule, unknown goes to the sandbox, malicious gets a documented deny.
media.alt: Flowchart from request arrival through evidence gathering to a decision diamond branching into three outcomes: approve with a scoped rule, detonate in the Testing Environment then ringfence, or deny with documented evidence.
Diagram of four labeled nodes (user, host, file, domain, IP) joined by labeled directed edges such as logged into, downloaded, and resolved to, illustrating graph vocabulary.
media.caption: Nodes are the things; edges are the relationships. Attackers move along the edges.
media.title: Graph vocabulary: nodes and edges

media.alt: Attack graph with four nodes in a chain: external attacker to VPN gateway to file server to customer database, with a dead-end branch to a printer, showing the shortest path to the crown jewel.
media.caption: The shortest path to the crown jewel is length 3. Break the choke point and the campaign dies.
media.title: Attack graph: shortest path to the crown jewels

media.alt: Seven kill-chain stages as connected graph nodes: reconnaissance, weaponization, delivery, exploitation, installation, command and control, actions. Three alerts are annotated at delivery, installation, and command and control.
media.caption: Three 'unrelated' alerts, one kill-chain subgraph. Correlate by shared entities, not by severity.
media.title: Kill chain as a graph

media.alt: A policy engine at the center of a small graph evaluates an access request from a finance user on an untrusted laptop to an R and D code server. The request is denied because there is no prior relationship edge and the device is untrusted.
media.caption: Valid credentials are not enough. The graph checks device trust, history, and relationships on every request.
media.title: Zero Trust runs on relationships
ML detection pipeline: telemetry to triage
media.caption: How raw telemetry becomes scored alerts: features feed the model, the model scores, analysts triage top-down — and analyst verdicts feed retraining.
media.alt: Flow diagram: telemetry sources feed feature extraction, which feeds an ML model, which outputs scored alerts into an analyst triage queue, with a feedback arrow for retraining.

media.title: UEBA: baseline vs deviation
media.caption: UEBA learns each user's normal hours, locations, and volumes, then scores deviations from that baseline.
media.alt: 24-hour timeline showing a shaded normal login window from 8 AM to 6 PM with normal logins inside it, and a red anomaly marker at 2:47 AM for a foreign login scoring 97 out of 100.

media.title: Indirect prompt injection attack flow
media.caption: An attacker hides instructions in data the agent retrieves; the agent mistakes data for instructions and misuses its tools.
media.alt: Attack flow diagram: hidden instruction in an email is read by an AI agent, which mistakes it for a command and calls a privileged tool, causing fraud; three defense boxes below: sanitize content, least-privilege tools, human approval.
